title: Lists that change
lesson:
A to-do list, a clinic queue, a player's inventory: lists that grow, shrink and change. The beginner way is to change the page directly: on "add", append an `<li>`; on "delete", find that `<li>` and remove it; on "done", add a class. It works for a while, then the page and your data **drift apart**: the counter says 3 but 4 items show, a deleted patient comes back after a refresh. Every app ends up needing the same fix.

**The fix: state plus render.**
- **State** is the truth, kept in plain JavaScript: `let queue = [{ id: 1, name: "Amina", seen: false }, ...]`.
- **render()** throws away what's on screen and redraws it entirely from the state.
- Every event follows one path: **change the state, then call render()**.

```
function render() {
  list.innerHTML = "";                  // 1. empty it (safe: "" holds no HTML)
  for (const p of queue) {              // 2. draw every item from state
    const li = document.createElement("li");
    li.textContent = p.name;
    if (p.seen) li.classList.add("seen");
    list.appendChild(li);
  }
  waiting.textContent = `${queue.filter((p) => !p.seen).length} waiting`;  // 3. summaries too
}
```

Now the page can't drift: it's always a picture of the state. (`list.replaceChildren()` also empties an element.) The classic bug is forgetting step 1, so every render adds a second copy of everything.

**Give items ids.** Don't identify items by their position: after a delete, positions shift and you'd toggle the wrong patient. Give each one an `id` from a counter (`nextId++`) and find it with `queue.find((p) => p.id === id)`.

**Buttons inside items.** When render builds a Delete button for an item, attach its listener right there; the arrow function remembers which item it belongs to:

```
del.addEventListener("click", () => removePatient(p.id));
```

**Changing state without surprises.** Two styles both work. You can change the array in place (`todo.done = !todo.done`, `queue.push(...)`), or build a new array and replace the old one:

```
queue = queue.filter((p) => p.id !== id);                         // remove
queue = queue.map((p) => (p.id === id ? { ...p, seen: !p.seen } : p));   // toggle
queue = [...queue, { id: nextId++, name, seen: false }];            // add
```

`{ ...p, seen: true }` copies an object and changes one field; `[...queue, x]` copies an array and adds one. Functions that return new arrays and never change their inputs are easy to test and can't break other code holding the old array. Game engines, React and most modern app tools are built on exactly this idea: state, a render from state, and events that change state.

notes: State is an array plus a counter for ids.
Every action changes the state and then calls render().
Items are found by id, so deleting one never confuses the others.
render empties the list and redraws everything, so the page always matches the state.

exercises.title: State changes
exercises.prompt: Write three pure functions for a clinic queue. A queue is an array like [{ id: 1, name: "Amina", seen: false }]. None of them may change the array or objects they're given; each returns a NEW array. addPatient(queue, name): trims the name; if it's blank return a copy of the queue unchanged; otherwise add { id, name, seen: false } at the end, where id is one more than the biggest id in the queue (1 if empty). toggleSeen(queue, id): flips seen for that id. removePatient(queue, id): leaves that id out.

tests.call: addPatient([{ id: 1, name: "Amina", seen: false }, { id: 4, name: "Juma", seen: true }], "Chebet")[2].id
tests.name: ids carry on from the biggest

tests.call: toggleSeen([{ id: 1, name: "Amina", seen: false }, { id: 2, name: "Juma", seen: false }], 2)
tests.name: toggle seen

tests.call: removePatient([{ id: 1, name: "Amina", seen: false }, { id: 2, name: "Juma", seen: false }], 1)
tests.name: remove
the originals are never changed

hints: The biggest id: queue.reduce((max, p) => Math.max(max, p.id), 0)
return [...queue, { id, name: clean, seen: false }];
toggle: queue.map((p) => (p.id === id ? { ...p, seen: !p.seen } : p)); remove: queue.filter((p) => p.id !== id)

quiz.q: Your render() works the first time, but each later call shows every item twice. Why?
choices: It doesn't empty the list before drawing

quiz.q: Why identify items by an id instead of their position in the array?
choices: Positions shift after a delete, so you'd change the wrong item
quiz.why: An id stays with its item no matter what else changes.

quiz.q: In the state-plus-render pattern, a click should…
choices: Change the state, then call render()
quiz.why: One path for every change keeps page and data in step.

choices: A new object copying p with seen set to true
quiz.why: Spread copies the fields; the later seen wins.

quiz.q: Why does del.addEventListener("click", () => deleteTodo(todo.id)) inside render's loop delete the right item?
choices: Each arrow function remembers the todo from its own loop round
quiz.why: A function made inside the loop keeps the variables of that round (a closure).

cards.a: Data lives in variables; render() redraws the page from it; events change the data then call render().

cards.q: Remove by id without changing the array?
Copy an array and add one?
